```json
{"claims":[
{"id":"c1","text":"Persistent SAEs separate a token-wise sparse activation a(t) from a persistent feature state h(t). Each feature has its own learned timescale and no predefined partition of temporal roles. Decoder-level attribution is preserved, and standard SAEs are a special case.","methods":["BatchTopK encoder produces a(t)","feature-wise state update h(t)=Phi_theta(h(t-1),a(t)) with h(0)=0 at sequence start","decoder reconstructs from h(t) (Eq. 3)","contrast with Temporal SAE (predefined high-level subset plus contrastive loss) and Lubana et al. (dense attention predictor)"],"results":["memoryless timescales make Eq. 3 reduce to Eq. 1","each state coordinate is tied to one decoder direction","inference cost per token is linear in dictionary size"],"conditions":["the update must act feature-wise","the restriction gives up expressiveness relative to general recurrent models"]},
{"id":"c2","text":"The state dynamics are constrained to be stable and non-degenerate. Sparsity applies only to the token-wise activation, not to the state.","methods":["timescales constrained to a contractive range","new evidence normalised","hard cap keeping effective memory finite","unconstrained parameter passed through a squashing function and initialised at an intermediate value","state L0 monitored during training"],"results":["the state h(t) is not necessarily sparse","at initialisation the model differs from a standard SAE only by moderate temporal smoothing","state L0 must be monitored because it is not directly controlled"],"conditions":["an effectively infinite timescale would freeze the first evidence and give ill-conditioned gradients"]},
{"id":"c3","text":"All four SAE families are trained under matched settings: width, sparsity, optimiser, steps and approximate token budget.","methods":["m=16,384 features, k=20, Adam with lr 3e-4","244,140 steps at about 2,048 activation tokens per step","Persistent SAE uses 8 contiguous sequences of length 256 from different documents, with reset state for each window","Temporal SAE uses adjacent token pairs","Matryoshka and Temporal SAEs use a 20%/80% partition","thresholded BatchTopK at inference"],"results":["about 5.0e8 tokens for the flat baselines","Persistent SAE gets 8×255=2,040 tokens per step, within 0.4% of the baseline","the thresholded form removes the dependence on batch composition"],"conditions":["models: Pythia-160M layer 8 and Gemma-2-2B layer 12","data: Pile Uncopyrighted"]},
{"id":"c4","text":"Temporal structure at the feature level is a separate question from correlation between hidden states. Measuring it requires controls for local versus global continuity and for confounds in dictionary geometry.","methods":["projections p_j = d_j^T x onto decoder directions","anchoring on activation events with normalisation","feature-wise context correction with one parameter per feature per lag","control that uses past activations from unrelated text","drop 16 prefix tokens and cap documents at 768 tokens"],"results":["projections are confounded because decoder directions are not orthogonal","aggregate medians conceal heterogeneity across features","a dense correction map would trivially exploit hidden-state correlation"],"conditions":["evaluate on held-out documents","exclude features with near-zero elevation"]},
{"id":"c5","text":"Interpretability is evaluated on the token-wise activations. The timescale quintiles are characterised by the token categories at which features receive new evidence.","methods":["Bills et al. autointerp with a gpt-4o-mini judge on a(t)","relative update frequency U_{q,c} over 5 timescale quintiles and 6 token categories, normalised by base rates"],"results":["for short-timescale features, a ≈ h, so scores are comparable to standard SAEs","a low token-level score for a long-timescale feature does not imply it is uninterpretable"],"conditions":["the judge sees short windows around high-activation tokens"]},
{"id":"c6","text":"Long-timescale persistent states are evaluated for whether they carry subject information. The labels are never used in training.","methods":["t-SNE of the final 20 tokens of 100 MMLU sequences from 5 subjects (descriptive only)","linear probe on spliced MMLU sequences using h(t)","features ranked by decreasing timescale, increasing timescale, random order, or a supervised oracle","fraction of features swept from 0.1% to 100%","macro ROC AUC","documents held out for test"],"results":["timescale vs random tests whether timescales carry relevance","Persistent vs baselines at matched budgets tests the effect of carrying state","the supervised ranking is a label-informed upper reference"],"conditions":["splicing forces the representation to update at boundaries"]},
{"id":"c7","text":"The persistent states are evaluated for long-context monitoring of indirect prompt injection, and for causal influence on a replay monitor.","methods":["AgentDojo banking, travel and workspace trajectories from Llama-3.3-70B","only failed attacks (security=false) as positives","Gemma-2-2B layer-12 replay monitor","logistic probe fit at d=0 and evaluated at d=50 to 350 without retraining","steering with the top k=128 probe-weighted decoder directions, scaled to rho=0.1 of the hidden-state norm, applied with both signs"],"results":["the yes-minus-no logit from prompting alone gives AUC 0.51","the fixed-probe protocol separates local detection from retention","the symmetric intervention removes direction-independent effects"],"conditions":["effects concern the external monitor, not the agent's actions"]},
{"id":"c8","text":"Limitations: each feature has a single timescale and a feature-wise recurrence. The model therefore cannot capture interactions between features or context-dependent resets, and token-level autointerp fits long-timescale features poorly.","methods":["feature-wise recurrence"],"results":["no clearing of state at a document boundary","the monitor is an external replay model"],"conditions":["evaluation covers 2 models, specific layers, and 3 AgentDojo domains"]}
],
"items":[
{"id":"q1","type":"failure","claims":["c6","c8"],"pair":null,"question":"In the spliced MMLU subject probing, would the longest-timescale Persistent SAE features be expected to predict the new subject accurately at the tokens just after a segment boundary, and why?","answer":"No. Their state decays only gradually and has no context-dependent reset, so just after a boundary it still largely reflects the previous segment's subject. Accuracy should recover only after enough new evidence has accumulated.","rubric":["Says the longest-timescale features would be inaccurate, or lag, right after a boundary","Reason: the state carries the previous subject forward because there is no reset; it only decays or integrates slowly","Condition: accuracy recovers as new-subject evidence accumulates over subsequent tokens"]},
{"id":"q2","type":"failure","claims":["c2","c6"],"pair":null,"question":"Suppose the hard cap on timescales were removed and a feature learned an effectively infinite timescale. Would that feature's state still track the current subject in spliced sequences, and why?","answer":"No. With an effectively infinite timescale the feature keeps the first evidence it receives for the rest of the sequence. It therefore cannot respond to the subject change at a splice boundary.","rubric":["Says no, it would not track the current subject","Reason: it retains the first evidence for the rest of the sequence and cannot respond to new context"]},
{"id":"q3","type":"failure","claims":["c3","c7"],"pair":null,"question":"Given the Persistent SAE's training windows, should one expect training to have shaped its timescales to retain the injection signal specifically at d=300–350 tokens? Why?","answer":"Not necessarily. Training used windows of 256 tokens (255 usable) with a reset state for each window. The reconstruction objective therefore never rewarded carrying information over more than about 255 tokens, so retention at 300–350 tokens is extrapolation beyond the training horizon.","rubric":["Says retention at 300–350 tokens is not directly optimised by training, or is uncertain","Reason: training sequences are only 256 tokens (255 usable) with a state reset, so no training signal spans more than about 255 tokens"]},
{"id":"q4","type":"failure","claims":["c4"],"pair":null,"question":"After feature j activates, its decoder-direction projection stays elevated for many tokens, but a strongly correlated feature fires throughout the same passage. Does this show that feature j itself persists, and why?","answer":"No. Decoder directions are not orthogonal, so the correlated feature's activity can raise the projection onto d_j. The measured persistence belongs to a residual-stream direction, not to feature j in isolation.","rubric":["Says no, the elevated projection does not establish feature j's own persistence","Reason: non-orthogonal decoder directions let a correlated active feature raise the projection, so persistence is a property of the direction"]},
{"id":"q5","type":"failure","claims":["c7"],"pair":null,"question":"A representation achieves high probe accuracy at d=0, but adding its probe-weighted direction with + and − signs shifts the monitor's yes-minus-no margin by the same amount. Would the causal analysis count it as influencing the monitor's judgement, and why?","answer":"No. The analysis takes the difference between the positive and negative interventions. Identical shifts cancel, which indicates only a generic, direction-independent perturbation effect, so the direction is decodable but not shown to be used.","rubric":["Says no causal influence is credited","Reason: the symmetric difference is about zero, so the effect is generic perturbation rather than alignment with the monitor's judgement"]},
{"id":"q6","type":"failure","claims":["c4"],"pair":null,"question":"Would a single dictionary-wide median decay curve computed over Pile documents reliably reveal a small set of long-lived features such as code-identifier trackers? Why or why not?","answer":"Probably not. The median summarises typical behaviour and can hide a minority of long-lived features. The Pile also mixes very different temporal regimes such as code and loosely related web fragments, so the aggregate averages them away. Per-band distributions or per-domain analyses are needed.","rubric":["Says no, or that it is unreliable","Reason: aggregate medians conceal heterogeneity across features and average over domains with different temporal regimes"]},
{"id":"q7","type":"why","claims":["c2","c3"],"pair":null,"question":"Why can the number of non-zero persistent-state coordinates per token exceed the BatchTopK budget of k=20, even though only about 20 features activate per token?","answer":"Sparsity is imposed only on the token-wise activation a(t). The state integrates activations from earlier tokens and decays rather than resetting. Features that fired at earlier positions therefore remain non-zero in h(t) alongside the current token's roughly 20 new activations.","rubric":["Notes that sparsity constrains a(t), not h(t)","Explains that earlier activations persist in the decaying state, so non-zero coordinates accumulate across tokens"]},
{"id":"q8","type":"why","claims":["c2","c5"],"pair":null,"question":"Why would the persistent state h(t) of a Persistent SAE tend to score better on the temporal smoothness metric than its own token-wise activation a(t), regardless of whether it captures meaningful context?","answer":"The state integrates sparse updates through a contractive, decaying recurrence. Consecutive values therefore differ less than the on/off sparse activations do. This smoothness is built into the dynamics, which is why smoothness must be read alongside FVE and cosine similarity.","rubric":["Says the state is smoother by construction","Reason: temporal integration or decay smooths token-to-token changes compared with sparse on/off activations","Condition: smoothness is only meaningful alongside reconstruction metrics"]},
{"id":"q9","type":"why","claims":["c6","c1"],"pair":null,"question":"Why does the subject probe for the Persistent SAE use the persistent state h(t) rather than the token-wise activation a(t)?","answer":"a(t) is non-zero only where new local evidence arrives, so at tokens without subject-specific words it carries little subject information. h(t) carries accumulated evidence forward, so it can encode the current subject at every token of a segment, which is what the spliced probing task requires.","rubric":["Says a(t) reflects only local, sparse evidence and is often zero at tokens lacking subject cues","Says h(t) carries accumulated subject evidence across tokens, matching the per-token temporal task"]},
{"id":"q10","type":"why","claims":["c3","c1"],"pair":null,"question":"Why does the Temporal SAE's training buffer return adjacent previous–next token pairs rather than flat shuffled tokens?","answer":"Its objective is contrastive alignment of its high-level features' activations across nearby tokens. Each training example therefore needs a neighbouring token from the same stream, which shuffled independent tokens cannot provide.","rubric":["Links the pairs to the Temporal SAE's contrastive objective across neighbouring tokens","Explains that shuffled tokens lack the neighbouring-token pairing that the objective needs"]},
{"id":"q11","type":"why","claims":["c3"],"pair":null,"question":"Why does using the thresholded form at inference matter more for the Persistent SAE than for the flat baselines?","answer":"The Persistent SAE's training batches contain only eight contiguous sequences, so the global top-kB selection allocated activations across positions in just a few documents. That allocation differs from both shuffled batches and from monitoring a single trajectory. A fixed threshold makes a(t) depend only on the current hidden state, which removes the dependence on batch composition.","rubric":["Says the Persistent SAE's batches are a few correlated documents, so exact BatchTopK allocation depends strongly on batch composition","Says the threshold makes a(t) a deterministic function of the current hidden state, independent of the batch"]},
{"id":"q12","type":"why","claims":["c6","c7","c1"],"pair":null,"question":"In the t-SNE and monitoring comparisons, why is the Temporal SAE represented by its predefined high-level group rather than its full dictionary?","answer":"The high-level group is the subset the Temporal SAE trains to be temporally consistent through its contrastive objective. It is the Temporal SAE's counterpart to a timescale-selected subset of Persistent SAE features, so the comparison is between the temporally structured components of each design.","rubric":["Says the high-level group is the part designated to carry temporal or contextual information (via the contrastive alignment)","Says it is the analogue of the timescale-selected Persistent SAE subset, so like is compared with like"]},
{"id":"q13","type":"why","claims":["c5","c1"],"pair":null,"question":"Why should autointerp scores for the shortest-timescale quintile of Persistent SAE features be directly comparable to BatchTopK feature scores, while scores for the longest quintile are not as informative?","answer":"Short-timescale features are nearly memoryless, so their state roughly equals their token-wise activation, and they behave like standard SAE features that local windows describe well. Long-timescale features accumulate evidence beyond the judge's short window, so a token-level score may miss their role.","rubric":["Short timescale: state ≈ activation, so the feature behaves like a standard SAE feature and local contexts suffice","Long timescale: relevance is spread beyond the judge's window, so a low score does not mean uninterpretable"]},
{"id":"q14","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c1"],"pair":"p1","question":"If every feature's timescale were set to be memoryless, would a Persistent SAE's reconstruction be identical to that of a standard Eq. 1 SAE with the same encoder and decoder?","answer":"Yes. With memoryless timescales h(t)=a(t), so Eq. 3 becomes W_dec a(t)+b_dec, which is exactly Eq. 1.","rubric":["Says yes, identical","Reason: memoryless means the state equals the token-wise activation, so Eq. 3 reduces to Eq. 1"]},
{"id":"q15","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c1","c2"],"pair":"p1","question":"If every feature's timescale were instead set at the hard cap, would a Persistent SAE's reconstruction be identical to that of a standard Eq. 1 SAE with the same encoder and decoder?","answer":"No. With long timescales the state accumulates evidence from earlier tokens, so h(t)≠a(t). The decoder then reconstructs from the history-dependent state rather than from the current activation alone.","rubric":["Says no","Reason: long-lived states include past activations, so h(t) differs from a(t) and the reconstruction depends on history"]},
{"id":"q16","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c1"],"pair":"p2","question":"If the timescales varied widely across features but the state update stayed feature-wise, would each reconstruction contribution remain attributable to a single decoder direction?","answer":"Yes. Under a feature-wise update, coordinate j depends only on feature j's history and is decoded only through d_j. Attribution holds whatever timescale each feature has.","rubric":["Says yes, attribution is preserved","Reason: a feature-wise update keeps each state coordinate tied to one dictionary element or decoder direction"]},
{"id":"q17","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c1"],"pair":"p2","question":"If the state update were replaced by a dense recurrence that mixes coordinates across features, would each reconstruction contribution remain attributable to a single decoder direction?","answer":"No. Mixing would make each state coordinate depend on other features' histories, so its contribution along d_j could no longer be read as the state of one nameable feature.","rubric":["Says no","Reason: cross-feature mixing breaks the tie between a state coordinate and a single feature's history, which is the paper's first requirement"]},
{"id":"q18","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c3"],"pair":"p3","question":"At inference, if the Persistent SAE kept exact BatchTopK selection, would a trajectory's token-wise activations a(t) depend on which other sequences were in the same batch?","answer":"Yes. Exact BatchTopK keeps the top kB entries globally across the batch, so a token's selected features depend on the competing pre-activations of other tokens in the batch.","rubric":["Says yes","Reason: global top-kB selection across the batch couples each token's activation to the batch composition"]},
{"id":"q19","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c3"],"pair":"p3","question":"At inference, if the Persistent SAE used the thresholded form with a fixed θ, would a trajectory's token-wise activations a(t) depend on which other sequences were in the same batch?","answer":"No. The thresholded form keeps pre-activations above a fixed θ estimated during training, so a(t) is a deterministic function of the current hidden state alone.","rubric":["Says no","Reason: a fixed threshold makes a(t) depend only on the current hidden state"]},
{"id":"q20","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c7"],"pair":"p4","question":"If the positive class consisted only of attacks with security=false, would high probe accuracy at late distances be good evidence that the representation retains the injection signal?","answer":"Yes, reasonably. In these runs the agent did not perform the attacker's action, so no overt malicious action is available as a cue. Accuracy at later distances must therefore come from a retained trace of the injection itself.","rubric":["Says yes","Reason: failed attacks contain no malicious action to serve as a downstream cue, so late accuracy reflects retention of the injection signal"]},
{"id":"q21","type":"counterfactual","claims":["c7"],"pair":"p4","question":"If the positive class instead included successful attacks (security=true), would high probe accuracy at late distances be good evidence that the representation retains the injection signal?","answer":"No. Successful attacks contain overt malicious actions such as money transfers later in the trajectory. A late-position probe could succeed by detecting those actions rather than a retained trace of the injection.","rubric":["Says no","Reason: the later overt malicious action gives a trivial cue that confounds retention"]},
{"id":"q22","type":"transfer","claims":["c7","c3"],"pair":null,"question":"A team must monitor agents whose action comes about 1,000 tokens after the injected span. Based on the paper's protocol and training setup, what representation should they try, and what caveat applies?","answer":"They should try the Persistent SAE state, especially the long-timescale subset, because it is designed to carry the signal forward. The caveat is that the paper evaluates only up to 350 tokens and trains on 256-token windows, so retention at 1,000 tokens is untested and should be checked with the same fixed-probe protocol.","rubric":["Recommends the long-timescale Persistent SAE state (or subset)","Caveat: evaluation stops at 350 tokens and training windows are 256 tokens, so 1,000-token retention is unverified"]},
{"id":"q23","type":"transfer","claims":["c5","c1"],"pair":null,"question":"An analyst wants to describe a Persistent SAE feature that fires on the substring 'function' in JavaScript code. Should they explain it from the token-wise activation in short windows or from its document-level persistent state, and why?","answer":"From the token-wise activation in short windows. The feature responds to a local substring, so its timescale is presumably short and h≈a. A document-level view adds little and may blur its description.","rubric":["Chooses token-wise activation with local windows","Reason: it is a local, token-level feature (likely short timescale, state ≈ activation), so a document-level view would blur the description"]},
{"id":"q24","type":"transfer","claims":["c8","c3"],"pair":null,"question":"A deployment feeds a Persistent SAE a single stream of many unrelated concatenated documents. What should the operators do at document boundaries, and why?","answer":"They should reset the state to h=0 at each boundary, as is done for each training window. The model has no learned context-dependent reset, so without manual resets the previous document's long-timescale state would carry into the next one.","rubric":["Recommends manually resetting the state to zero at document boundaries","Reason: the feature-wise recurrence cannot clear the state itself, so the previous document's state would leak; training also used resets"]},
{"id":"q25","type":"transfer","claims":["c3"],"pair":null,"question":"A team retrains the Persistent SAE with context length 512 and wants to stay matched to the 2,048-token-per-step baselines. How many sequences per step should they use, and how many usable tokens results?","answer":"Four sequences per step. After dropping the beginning-of-sequence token, 4×511=2,044 usable tokens results, close to 2,048. Keeping eight sequences would give 4,088 tokens and break the match.","rubric":["Says 4 sequences per step","Gives about 2,044 usable tokens (4×511), and notes that 8 sequences would roughly double the budget"]},
{"id":"q26","type":"transfer","claims":["c4","c3"],"pair":null,"question":"If the feature-wise context correction diagnostic were applied to the paper's Matryoshka SAE at one lag, how many correction parameters would be fitted, and why is that count desirable?","answer":"16,384, one per feature. Having only one parameter per feature lets any gain be attributed to specific features, and its sign shows the direction of the effect. A dense map would instead have far more parameters and would exploit general hidden-state correlation.","rubric":["Says 16,384 parameters (one per feature)","Reason: one parameter per feature keeps any gain attributable to individual features, unlike a dense map"]},
{"id":"q27","type":"transfer","claims":["c6","c3"],"pair":null,"question":"A team wants an unsupervised subject summary using the smallest fraction swept in the probing analysis. About how many Persistent SAE features is that, and which comparison tells them whether ranking by timescale is worth using?","answer":"0.1% of 16,384 is about 16 features. The decreasing-timescale ranking should be compared against the averaged random rankings at that budget. The supervised ranking shows how far it falls from a label-informed ceiling.","rubric":["Says about 16 features (0.1% of 16,384)","Says to compare the decreasing-timescale ranking with random rankings (the supervised oracle serves as a reference ceiling)"]},
{"id":"q28","type":"connect","claims":["c6","c1"],"pair":null,"question":"If the decreasing-timescale ranking had performed no better than random rankings in spliced subject probing, which conclusion would lose support?","answer":"The conclusion that the learned timescale parameters carry information about which features are relevant to subject, i.e. that long-timescale states track subject information. Persistent states might still encode subject, but timescale would not be a useful selection criterion.","rubric":["Names the claim that timescale parameters indicate subject relevance (long-timescale states track subject)","Notes that the timescale-vs-random comparison is what tests this claim"]},
{"id":"q29","type":"connect","claims":["c7"],"pair":null,"question":"If the monitor's own yes-minus-no answer logit had achieved an AUC near 0.9 instead of 0.51, which design choice of the case study would lose its stated justification?","answer":"The choice to train internal linear probes on representations rather than rely on prompting the monitor. The near-chance 0.51 AUC is what motivates internal monitors.","rubric":["Identifies training internal probes instead of prompting","Reason: prompting would already be informative, removing the motivation given by the 0.51 AUC"]},
{"id":"q30","type":"connect","claims":["c7","c1"],"pair":null,"question":"If the fixed d=0 probe on the Persistent SAE state had lost accuracy with distance as quickly as the raw hidden state did, which motivating claim of the paper would be undermined?","answer":"The claim that representations which explicitly carry state forward are natural candidates for long-context monitoring, i.e. that persistence helps retain the security-relevant signal until the agent acts. Local detection near d=0 would be unaffected.","rubric":["Identifies the claim that persistent states support long-context retention or monitoring","Notes this concerns retention over distance, not local detection at d=0"]},
{"id":"q31","type":"connect","claims":["c4","c1"],"pair":null,"question":"If the Persistent SAE's timescale parameters showed no relation to projection-based persistence measured in the hidden states, which interpretation of those parameters would lose support?","answer":"The interpretation that the timescales reflect measurable persistence in the underlying representation. They would then be model properties only, not evidence that the corresponding features are long-lived in the data.","rubric":["Says the meaningfulness of timescales as reflecting real persistence in hidden states would be undermined","Reason: projection-based measures are the check of whether the parameters correspond to observable persistence"]},
{"id":"q32","type":"connect","claims":["c2","c3"],"pair":null,"question":"If the state L0 in Figure 4 had grown steadily without bound over training, which design requirement would appear violated, and what downstream problem would follow?","answer":"The stability or boundedness requirement, implemented by the contractive timescale range and normalisation. Decoder inputs would then vary in scale with position, which complicates optimisation and makes late-position reconstructions incomparable with early ones.","rubric":["Identifies the stability / bounded-state requirement (contractive parameterisation)","Gives the consequence: decoder input scale depends on position, harming optimisation or comparability"]},
{"id":"q33","type":"connect","claims":["c4"],"pair":null,"question":"In the context correction experiment, if past activations drawn from unrelated text recovered as much reconstruction error as the true document history, which conclusion would that undermine?","answer":"The conclusion that an atemporal SAE leaves genuine feature-level temporal information unused. The gain would come from the marginal statistics of the activations, not from the document's actual history.","rubric":["Identifies the claim that standard SAEs leave feature-level temporal information unused","Reason: the control preserves marginal statistics but removes the genuine history, so equal gains imply no history-specific signal"]},
{"id":"q34","type":"connect","claims":["c1","c3"],"pair":null,"question":"If the Persistent SAE's FVE had been far below BatchTopK under the matched budget, which requirement stated in the paper would it fail, and why would that matter for its use?","answer":"It would fail the first requirement that an SAE extension should not degrade the decomposition it extends. An extension that trades fidelity for temporal structure would be hard to justify against BatchTopK and Matryoshka on standard criteria.","rubric":["Identifies the requirement that the extension not degrade reconstruction relative to atemporal baselines","Reason: under matched budgets, lower fidelity would undermine justification for using it"]},
{"id":"q35","type":"scope","claims":["c7"],"pair":null,"question":"Does the paper show that Persistent SAE states support prompt-injection monitoring across all AgentDojo domains? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.","answer":"Not settled. AgentDojo includes workspace, Slack, travel and banking, but the monitoring data uses only banking, travel and workspace trajectories, so Slack is untested.","rubric":["Answers not settled","Reason: only banking, travel and workspace are used; Slack is excluded"]},
{"id":"q36","type":"scope","claims":["c3","c6","c7"],"pair":null,"question":"Does the paper establish that its findings about Persistent SAEs hold for large frontier models and for any layer? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.","answer":"Not settled. All SAEs are trained only on Pythia-160M layer 8 and Gemma-2-2B layer 12, and the monitor is Gemma-2-2B layer 12, so other models and layers are untested.","rubric":["Answers not settled","Reason: only Pythia-160M layer 8 and Gemma-2-2B layer 12 are used"]},
{"id":"q37","type":"scope","claims":["c2","c3"],"pair":null,"question":"Does the paper's design guarantee that the persistent state h(t) has at most about k=20 active features per token, like the baselines? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.","answer":"Contradicted. Sparsity is imposed only on the token-wise activation, and the accumulated state is explicitly not necessarily sparse. Its L0 is uncontrolled and must be monitored.","rubric":["Answers contradicted","Reason: the k budget applies to a(t); h(t) integrates updates and is not directly sparsity-constrained"]},
{"id":"q38","type":"scope","claims":["c8","c1"],"pair":null,"question":"Can a Persistent SAE represent one feature's activation clearing or resetting another feature's state, for example a boundary feature resetting a topic feature? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.","answer":"Contradicted. The state update is feature-wise, so each coordinate depends only on its own feature's history. Interactions between features and context-dependent resets are named as limitations.","rubric":["Answers contradicted","Reason: the feature-wise recurrence means no cross-feature interactions or context-dependent resets"]},
{"id":"q39","type":"scope","claims":["c1"],"pair":null,"question":"Is the Persistent SAE more expressive as a sequence model than general recurrent or state-space models? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.","answer":"Contradicted. It restricts the carried state so that each coordinate is tied to a single dictionary element, which the paper says sacrifices expressiveness relative to general recurrent models in exchange for interpretability.","rubric":["Answers contradicted","Reason: the feature-wise restriction trades expressiveness for interpretability"]},
{"id":"q40","type":"scope","claims":["c2","c5"],"pair":null,"question":"Does the protocol let the paper conclude that Persistent SAE features are smoother than Temporal SAE high-level features on an equal footing? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.","answer":"Not settled. The Temporal SAE's groups are predefined, while the Persistent SAE's grouping is derived from its own timescales, so the paper calls the comparison asymmetric by design. The state is also smooth partly by construction, so smoothness must be read with FVE and cosine similarity.","rubric":["Answers not settled","Reason: the grouping is asymmetric (predefined vs timescale-derived), and smoothness is only meaningful alongside fidelity"]}
]}
```

{"items": [
{"id": "q41", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c2", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "Suppose the Persistent SAE's state update kept its contractive timescales but dropped the normalisation of new evidence. For a long-timescale feature that fires often, would the decoder still see inputs on a consistent scale across positions, and why?", "answer": "No. Without normalisation, each new activation adds evidence on top of what the slowly decaying state already holds. A frequently firing long-timescale feature's state would therefore climb well above the scale of the token-wise activations, and how far it climbs would depend on position and firing history. Reconstructions at late positions would then not be comparable to early ones, which is the problem the paper's stability requirement is meant to prevent.", "rubric": ["Concludes that the scale would not stay consistent: the state can grow beyond the activation scale, depending on position or firing frequency.", "Explains that accumulated evidence is not rescaled, so repeated activations pile up under slow decay, and links this to the stated need for the decoder to see inputs on a consistent scale or for late reconstructions to be comparable to early ones."]},
{"id": "q42", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c2", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "If the unconstrained timescale parameters were initialised deep in a saturated region of the squashing function rather than at an intermediate value, would features reliably learn their own heterogeneous timescales during training? Why?", "answer": "Probably not. In a saturated region, the gradients with respect to the timescale parameters are vanishingly small. Timescales would then barely move from their starting value, so features would not spread to the range of timescales the paper relies on. The paper chose an intermediate initialisation precisely so that each timescale could move in either direction.", "rubric": ["Concludes that timescales would tend to stay stuck near their initial value and would not diversify.", "Reason: gradients through a saturated squashing function are vanishingly small, unlike at the intermediate initialisation, which lets timescales move in either direction."]},
{"id": "q43", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c6"], "pair": null, "question": "In the spliced MMLU probing, suppose test tokens could come from the same source questions as training tokens. Would a high macro ROC AUC still be good evidence that a representation tracks the current subject? Why?", "answer": "No. If test tokens shared source questions with training tokens, the probe could score well by recognising memorised content from specific questions rather than by reading a generalisable subject signal. Holding out entire source documents is what rules this out.", "rubric": ["Concludes that the AUC would no longer be good evidence of subject tracking.", "Reason: the probe could exploit memorised content of shared source questions; holding out whole documents is the safeguard against this."]},
{"id": "q44", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c7", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "In the steering analysis, suppose each representation's steering vector were built from all features with non-zero probe coefficients rather than the top k=128. A direction assembled from more features could produce a larger effect simply by spanning more of the residual stream. Fixing k=128 is what equalises this across representations.", "rubric": ["Concludes that the comparison would be unfair or confounded.", "Reason: the dense Persistent state would let its direction draw on many more features, and more features can yield larger effects just by spanning more of the residual stream; the fixed k=128 prevents this."]},
{"id": "q45", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c7"], "pair": null, "question": "If steering interventions were added with a fixed absolute norm instead of a fraction ρ=0.1 of the hidden-state norm, would differences in the effect on the monitor's logit margin across distances and trajectories be interpretable? Why?", "answer": "No. Residual-stream norms vary across positions and trajectories. A fixed absolute perturbation would be relatively large where the norm is small and small where it is large. Changes in effect with distance could then reflect norm differences rather than how the direction's causal effect transfers.", "rubric": ["Concludes that the effects would not be comparably interpretable.", "Reason: residual norms vary by position and trajectory, so a fixed absolute size gives perturbations of different relative strength; relative scaling keeps them comparable."]},
{"id": "q46", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c4"], "pair": null, "question": "If the feature-wise context correction were fitted and scored on the same documents without regularisation, could a measured reduction in reconstruction error be trusted as evidence of feature-level temporal information? Why?", "answer": "No. The expected gains are small relative to total reconstruction error. Without held-out evaluation and regularisation, parameters for rarely active features could overfit, producing improvements that reflect fitting noise rather than a genuine relationship with the document's history.", "rubric": ["Concludes that the reduction could not be trusted.", "Reason: overfitting, especially of rarely active features, can produce gains comparable to the small true effect; the paper requires disjoint held-out documents and regularisation."]},
{"id": "q47", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c3", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "Suppose Persistent SAE training windows started at arbitrary mid-document points, with the state still set to h(0)=0. For long-timescale features, would the state at early window positions faithfully reflect the context, and why?", "answer": "No. The zero initial state would assert that there is no preceding context, while the hidden states already encode the earlier document. This is why the paper takes sequences from document beginnings where possible.", "rubric": ["Concludes that early states would misrepresent (understate) the context.", "Reason: h(0)=0 means absence of preceding context, but a truncated window has real preceding context in the hidden state; slow features need many tokens to catch up."]},
{"id": "q48", "type": "why", "claims": ["c3", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "Why does the Persistent SAE draw its 8 training sequences per step from different documents, rather than using one contiguous stretch of about 2,040 tokens from a single document?", "answer": "Tokens within a sequence are correlated, so a batch from one document would be highly correlated and would destabilise optimisation compared with shuffled baselines. Also, the batch-level top-kB selection would then allocate activations only among positions of a single document. Drawing from different documents limits both effects while still giving contiguous context for the state.", "rubric": ["Identifies within-sequence correlation as the problem that multiple documents reduce.", "Notes that BatchTopK's global selection allocates activations across the batch, so a single-document batch would concentrate the sparsity budget within one document (or otherwise ties the choice to batch composition)."]},
{"id": "q49", "type": "why", "claims": ["c2", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "Why does a freshly initialised Persistent SAE behave like a standard BatchTopK SAE with only moderate temporal smoothing, rather than like a long-memory model?", "answer": "The timescales start at an intermediate value, so features neither copy activations exactly nor hold them for long. New evidence is normalised, so the state stays on the scale of the token-wise activations. The decoder therefore sees a lightly smoothed version of essentially standard SAE activations.", "rubric": ["Cites the intermediate initial timescale (neither memoryless nor long-lived).", "Cites normalisation of new evidence, which keeps the state on the same scale as the activations, so the decoder input resembles smoothed standard activations."]},
{"id": "q50", "type": "why", "claims": ["c1", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "Why can a monitor based on the Persistent SAE state run online over an arbitrarily long agent trajectory without storing the past hidden states?", "answer": "The state update h(t)=Φ(h(t−1),a(t)) depends only on the previous state and the current token-wise activation, and it acts feature-wise. Each token therefore needs one update costing time linear in dictionary size, and the history is summarised in h(t−1).", "rubric": ["States that h(t) depends only on h(t−1) and the current a(t), a recurrent summary.", "Notes that the per-token cost is linear in dictionary size, so no stored history or attention over past tokens is needed."]},
{"id": "q51", "type": "why", "claims": ["c1", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Why can a long-timescale Persistent SAE feature contribute to the reconstruction at a token where its token-wise activation a_j(t) is zero?", "answer": "The decoder reconstructs from the persistent state h(t), not from a(t). A long-timescale feature's state retains evidence from earlier activations, so h_j(t) can remain positive and add its decoder direction even when no new evidence arrives at token t.", "rubric": ["States that reconstruction uses h(t), per Eq. 3.", "Explains that h_j retains decaying past evidence, so it can be non-zero while a_j(t)=0."]},
{"id": "q52", "type": "why", "claims": ["c7", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "Why does the monitoring protocol place checkpoints in benign trajectories at the position matched to the end of an injected span, rather than at arbitrary positions?", "answer": "Hidden-state statistics vary with position. If positive and negative checkpoints sat at systematically different positions, a probe could separate them using positional drift rather than injection content. Matching positions keeps the distance-based comparison aligned across classes.", "rubric": ["Concludes that matching avoids a positional confound between classes.", "Reason: representations drift with position, so mismatched positions could give a spurious cue; matching keeps offsets d comparable."]},
{"id": "q53", "type": "why", "claims": ["c1", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "Why is the paper's check on whether temporal structure is meaningful for the Temporal SAE phrased in terms of its predefined groups differing in projection-based persistence, rather than per-feature agreement as for the Persistent SAE?", "answer": "The Temporal SAE has no per-feature timescale; temporal roles come only from the fixed high-level/low-level partition. The only model-side quantity to relate to measured persistence is therefore group membership, whereas the Persistent SAE exposes a timescale parameter for every feature.", "rubric": ["States that the Temporal SAE lacks per-feature timescales and has only a predefined partition.", "Concludes that its temporal assumptions can only be checked at group level, unlike the Persistent SAE's per-feature parameters."]},
{"id": "q54", "type": "why", "claims": ["c4"], "pair": null, "question": "Why is excluding early token positions particularly important for measuring how a projection decays over lags after an activation event?", "answer": "Lag comparisons set the projection at the anchor against projections at later positions. Hidden states at the first positions have atypical statistics, and statistics drift with position. Anchors near the start would therefore mix genuine decay with positional effects. Dropping the prefix and capping document length reduces this confound.", "rubric": ["Identifies positional drift or atypical early-position statistics as the confound.", "Explains that lagged measurements compare different positions, so early anchors would conflate positional change with persistence."]},
{"id": "q55", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c4"], "pair": "p1", "question": "In the context correction diagnostic, if each feature's correction used only its own past activation along its own decoder direction, could a reduction in reconstruction error be attributed to specific features?", "answer": "Yes. With one parameter per feature acting along that feature's own direction, any gain can be traced to particular features. The sign of each parameter shows whether past activation predicts a positive or negative contribution.", "rubric": ["Answers yes.", "Reason: one parameter per feature along its own direction keeps the effect attributable to individual features."]},
{"id": "q56", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c4"], "pair": "p1", "question": "In the context correction diagnostic, if the correction were an arbitrary dense linear map from all past activations to the current hidden state, could a reduction in reconstruction error be attributed to specific features?", "answer": "No. A dense map could exploit the known correlation between consecutive hidden states through mixtures of many features. {"id": "q58", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c3"], "pair": "p2", "question": "Under exact BatchTopK training, can the distribution of active features across token positions differ between the Persistent SAE's contiguous-sequence batches and the flat baselines' shuffled batches?", "answer": "Yes. {"id": "q59", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c3"], "pair": "p3", "question": "If the Persistent SAE used 8 sequences of length 256 per step, with the beginning-of-sequence position excluded, would its activation tokens per step stay within 1% of the flat baselines' 2,048?", "answer": "Yes. {"id": "q60", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c3"], "pair": "p3", "question": "If the Persistent SAE used 8 sequences of length 128 per step, with the beginning-of-sequence position excluded, would its activation tokens per step stay within 1% of the flat baselines' 2,048?", "answer": "No. It would get 8×127=1,016 tokens per step, about half the baseline. {"id": "q61", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c6"], "pair": "p4", "question": "If the probing sequences were spliced from segments of different MMLU subjects, would a representation have to update what it encodes mid-sequence to score well?", "answer": "Yes. {"id": "q62", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c6"], "pair": "p4", "question": "If each probing sequence instead contained a single MMLU subject throughout, would a representation have to update what it encodes mid-sequence to score well?", "answer": "No. The label would be constant within each sequence, so no boundary update would be needed. {"id": "q63", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": null, "question": "In some timescale quintile, 30% of feature updates fall on nouns, while nouns make up 20% of corpus tokens. {"id": "q64", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c7"], "pair": null, "question": "At an intervention position where the hidden-state norm is 80, what norm does the paper's steering vector have, and how many decoder directions are combined into it?", "answer": "The vector is scaled to ρ=0.1 of the norm, giving 8, and it combines the k=128 features with the largest absolute probe coefficients. {"id": "q65", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c6", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "A team applies the paper's spliced subject-probing protocol to the Lubana et al. predictive decomposition. {"id": "q66", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c3", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "In the paper's 16,384-feature Temporal SAE, roughly how many features make up the high-level group that is used in the t-SNE and monitoring comparisons?", "answer": "About 3,277 features (20% of 16,384), since the Temporal SAE uses the 20%/80% partition and the high-level group is the 20% subset.", "rubric": ["Gives about 3,277 (≈3,276.8), i.e. 20% of 16,384.", "Ties this to the 20%/80% partition with the high-level group as the 20% subset."]},
{"id": "q67", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c1", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "An analyst sees that feature j has a large persistent state at token 400 but a_j=0 there. {"id": "q68", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c4", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "A team has only a frozen BatchTopK SAE and wants a cheap test of whether a persistent formulation could exploit feature-level history, without training a Persistent SAE. {"id": "q69", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c5", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "If every timescale quintile had shown U_{q,c}≈1 for all six token categories, which expectation in the paper would lack support?", "answer": "The expectation that meaningful timescales are reflected in where features receive new evidence, for example short versus long features preferring content words versus punctuation or function words. {"id": "q70", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c6"], "pair": null, "question": "If the Persistent SAE state had matched the BatchTopK, Matryoshka and Temporal SAE representations at every feature budget in spliced probing, which question would get a negative answer?", "answer": "Whether carrying state forward changes what a fixed number of features can encode about the current subject. {"id": "q71", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c7", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "If the short-timescale and long-timescale subsets of the Persistent SAE state had shown identical accuracy curves across distance in the fixed-probe evaluation, which question posed by the case study would get a negative answer?", "answer": "Whether fast and slow components of the persistent representation divide the labour between immediate detection near d=0 and long-context retention. {"id": "q72", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c1", "c6", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "If all learned timescales had collapsed to memoryless during training, which parts of the evaluation would lose their basis for distinguishing the Persistent SAE from a standard SAE?", "answer": "The Persistent SAE would reduce to a standard SAE (Eq. 3 equals Eq. 1), so h(t)=a(t). {"id": "q73", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c3", "c5", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "If the thresholded inference form had produced token-wise activations that differed substantially from the training-time BatchTopK selection, which downstream evaluations of the Persistent SAE would be affected?", "answer": "All of them. {"id": "q74", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c1", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "If the Temporal SAE's predefined high-level group had matched the long-timescale Persistent SAE subset in subject information, which motivation for the paper's design would be weakened?", "answer": "The motivation that locating timescales in individual features, rather than in a predefined partition, offers an advantage. {"id": "q75", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c4", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "If decoder-direction projections after standard SAE activations had shown no elevation beyond what local continuity explains, once the control disrupting global continuity was applied, which motivating claim would weaken?", "answer": "The claim that atemporal SAE features carry document-level temporal information that a decomposition could expose per feature. {"id": "q76", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c6"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the t-SNE visualisation, on its own, establish that the timescale-selected Persistent SAE state encodes subject better than BatchTopK features? {"id": "q77", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c1", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper hold that a good decomposition should push features toward slow, long timescales? {"id": "q78", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c3"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the matched setup mean all four SAE families were trained on identical token activations? {"id": "q79", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c6"], "pair": null, "question": "Would strong spliced-probing performance of the long-timescale Persistent SAE features show that individual features each track a subject? {"id": "q80", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c1"], "pair": null, "question": "Does running a Persistent SAE require reprocessing the whole token history at each new token, making per-token cost grow with sequence length? {"id": "q81", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c6", "c8"], "pair": null, "question": "Do the paper's MMLU analyses show that persistent states organise text by subject across MMLU's 57 subjects? {"id": "q88", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c1", "c3"], "pair": null, "question": "If the Persistent SAE were trained on shuffled token activations like the flat baselines, would its learned timescales describe how long feature information persists in real text? Why?", "answer": "No. With shuffled tokens, the state at each token would integrate activations from unrelated preceding tokens, not the actual preceding context. Whatever timescales were learned would therefore not reflect persistence in real documents. The paper requires contiguous sequences precisely so that the state reflects the true history.", "rubric": ["States that the timescales would not describe real persistence", "Explains that the state would integrate unrelated tokens instead of the actual preceding context, which is why contiguous sequences are required"]},
{"id": "q89", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c1", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "In the monitoring evaluation, should the Persistent SAE's token-wise activation a(t), by construction, retain the injection signal at d=350 as well as its state h(t)? Why?", "answer": "No, not by construction. a(t) is computed from the current hidden state alone and carries nothing forward; it only marks new evidence at the current token. h(t) integrates past activations through each feature's timescale. Any retention in a(t) would have to come from the hidden state itself, as for the atemporal baselines.", "rubric": ["States that a(t) is not built to retain the signal as h(t) is", "Explains that a(t) is a token-wise function of the current hidden state with no carried state, whereas h(t) accumulates past evidence through the feature timescales"]},
{"id": "q90", "type": "why", "claims": ["c3", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "The agent trajectories were generated by Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct. Why does the monitoring case study replay them through Gemma-2-2B instead of reading the agent's own activations?", "answer": "The paper's SAEs, including the Persistent SAE, were trained on Gemma-2-2B layer-12 (and Pythia) activations, not on Llama-3.3-70B. To probe and steer with those dictionaries, the trajectories must be read by the model and layer the SAEs were trained on.", "rubric": ["States that the SAEs were trained on Gemma-2-2B layer 12, not on the agent model", "Explains that the SAE representations and decoder directions can only be used on activations from the model and layer they were trained on, hence the replay"]},
{"id": "q91", "type": "why", "claims": ["c7"], "pair": null, "question": "The raw hidden state is one of the representations probed for injection retention. Why can the paper's causal intervention not be built for it in the same way as for the SAE representations?", "answer": "The steering vector is built by choosing the k=128 features with the largest probe coefficients and combining their decoder columns. The raw hidden state has no dictionary features or decoder columns. Its probe weights are dense coordinates, not a top-128 set of decoder directions.", "rubric": ["States that the construction needs SAE features with decoder directions, which the raw hidden state lacks", "Refers to the top-k=128 probe-weighted decoder columns as the construction that cannot be applied"]},
{"id": "q92", "type": "why", "claims": ["c1", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Why might a Persistent SAE spend fewer of its token-wise activations than a standard SAE on a property that holds across a whole passage, such as its topic, even under the same k=20 budget?", "answer": "A standard SAE reconstructs each token only from that token's activations, so a passage-wide feature must be reselected at every token to contribute. In a Persistent SAE, a feature with a long timescale keeps contributing through its state h(t) after it fires. It needs new activation only occasionally, which frees budget for other features.", "rubric": ["States that the Persistent SAE needs to reactivate the feature less often", "Explains that the decoder reads from the persistent state, so a long-timescale feature keeps contributing between activations, whereas a standard SAE must fire it at every token"]},
{"id": "q93", "type": "why", "claims": ["c6", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "In the t-SNE comparison, why is the Persistent SAE represented by a subset of its state selected by timescale rather than its full state?", "answer": "Subject is a slowly varying, contextual property, so the long-timescale coordinates are the ones expected to carry it. The full state also contains short-timescale features that track token-level lexical events, and these would add variation unrelated to subject.", "rubric": ["States that the subset targets the long-timescale coordinates expected to carry contextual or subject information", "Explains that short-timescale features mostly reflect token-level cues and would dilute subject structure"]},
{"id": "q94", "type": "why", "claims": ["c1", "c3"], "pair": null, "question": "Why does the Persistent SAE produce its token-wise activation a(t) with the same BatchTopK encoder (thresholded at inference) as the baselines, rather than with a sparsity scheme of its own?", "answer": "Using the same encoder and sparsity budget means the only difference from a standard SAE is the downstream state and decoding from h(t). The comparison then isolates the effect of carrying state, and memoryless timescales recover the standard SAE exactly.", "rubric": ["States that it isolates the persistent state as the only difference", "Links this to the matched comparison with the baselines or to standard SAEs being a special case"]},
{"id": "q95", "type": "why", "claims": ["c6"], "pair": null, "question": "In spliced subject probing, why might one expect the Persistent SAE state to do relatively well on tokens deep inside a segment that contain no subject-specific words?", "answer": "The state h(t) accumulates evidence from earlier tokens in the segment, so subject information picked up from earlier cues can persist into tokens without such cues. A token-wise representation must rely on whatever local lexical cues happen to appear near each token, and here there are none.", "rubric": ["States that the persistent state can still carry the subject there", "Explains that h(t) integrates evidence from earlier tokens, whereas token-wise representations depend on local cues that are absent at such tokens"]},
{"id": "q96", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c6"], "pair": "p1", "question": "If the supervised feature score in Eq. 8 is computed on the training split, would the supervised ranking use the labels of test tokens?", "answer": "No. The score is computed from training-split states and labels only, and test documents are held out. The ranking is label-informed but does not draw on the test labels.", "rubric": ["Answers no", "Explains that the score uses only training-split labels and the test documents are held out"]},
{"id": "q97", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c6"], "pair": "p1", "question": "If the supervised feature score in Eq. 8 were instead computed on the test split, would the supervised ranking use the labels of test tokens?", "answer": "Yes. Feature selection would then be driven by the very labels the probe is scored on. This leaks test information and would inflate the reference curve beyond a fair label-informed upper reference.", "rubric": ["Answers yes", "Explains that selection would use the labels being evaluated, leaking test information and inflating the reference"]},
{"id": "q98", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c3", "c2"], "pair": "p2", "question": "During Persistent SAE training with context length 256, would a document of exactly 256 tokens, taken from its beginning, yield any window whose zero initial state is set at an arbitrary mid-document point?", "answer": "No. The document fits in one window that starts at the document beginning, so h(0)=0 matches the true absence of preceding context.", "rubric": ["Answers no", "Explains that it fits in a single window starting at the document beginning, so the reset matches the real absence of preceding context"]},
{"id": "q99", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c3", "c2"], "pair": "p2", "question": "During Persistent SAE training with context length 256, would a 700-token document yield any window whose zero initial state is set at an arbitrary mid-document point?", "answer": "Yes. A document longer than the context length is split into later windows, which are treated as fresh sequences with a reset state. Those windows start mid-document even though real preceding context exists.", "rubric": ["Answers yes", "Explains that subsequent windows of longer documents are reset to zero although they begin mid-document"]},
{"id": "q100", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c6"], "pair": "p3", "question": "Under the supervised ranking, would a feature whose persistent state is equally large on every token, regardless of subject, rank near the top for any subject?", "answer": "No. Eq. 8 is the difference between the mean state on subject c and on all other subjects. For a feature that is equally high everywhere this difference is about zero, so it ranks low for every subject.", "rubric": ["Answers no", "Explains that Eq. 8 measures the difference between mean states inside and outside the subject, which is about zero for a uniformly high feature"]},
{"id": "q101", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c6"], "pair": "p3", "question": "Under the supervised ranking, would a feature whose persistent state is large mainly on abstract algebra tokens rank near the top for some subject?", "answer": "Yes. Its Eq. 8 score for abstract algebra is large and positive, so it ranks high in that subject's list. The round-robin interleaving puts that subject's top features early in the global ordering.", "rubric": ["Answers yes, for abstract algebra", "Explains that the in-subject minus out-of-subject mean difference is large, and round-robin interleaving places that subject's top features early"]},
{"id": "q102", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c1", "c3"], "pair": "p4", "question": "If the Temporal SAE's predefined high-level group were smoother than its low-level group, could that gap reflect an explicit temporal training signal applied to that group?", "answer": "Yes. The Temporal SAE applies a contrastive objective that aligns its high-level group's activations across nearby tokens, which is a direct training pressure toward smoothness.", "rubric": ["Answers yes", "Cites the contrastive objective that aligns high-level activations across adjacent tokens"]},
{"id": "q103", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c1", "c3"], "pair": "p4", "question": "If the Matryoshka SAE's predefined high-level group were smoother than its low-level group, could that gap reflect an explicit temporal training signal applied to that group?", "answer": "No. The Matryoshka SAE has no temporal prior: it trains nested dictionaries with uniform reconstruction weights on shuffled tokens. Any smoothness gap would have to come from what the nested structure leads the high-level group to encode, not from a temporal objective.", "rubric": ["Answers no", "Explains that Matryoshka has no temporal objective (nested dictionaries, shuffled tokens, uniform weights), so any gap arises indirectly"]},
{"id": "q104", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c3"], "pair": null, "question": "Using the paper's numbers, how many activation tokens does the Persistent SAE process over its full training run, and how many fewer is that than the flat baselines?", "answer": "2,040 × 244,140 = 498,045,600 tokens, about 4.98e8. That is 1,953,120 fewer than the baselines' 499,998,720, a shortfall of about 0.4%.", "rubric": ["Gives about 498,045,600 (≈4.98e8) tokens", "Gives a difference of about 1.95 million tokens (≈0.4%) from 499,998,720"]},
{"id": "q105", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c3"], "pair": null, "question": "With m=16,384 for both models, how overcomplete is the dictionary relative to the hidden width for the Pythia-160M SAEs compared with the Gemma-2-2B SAEs?", "answer": "Pythia layer 8 has d=768, so the expansion is about 16,384/768 ≈ 21.3×. {"id": "q106", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c7", "c3", "c8"], "pair": null, "question": "A team wants to use Persistent SAE states to monitor the Llama-3.3-70B agent's own internal representations and to steer the agent's actions. Can they reuse the paper's trained SAEs and causal results directly? What would they need instead?", "answer": "No. The paper's SAEs were trained on Gemma-2-2B layer 12 (and Pythia), and its interventions affect only an external replay monitor's judgement, not the agent's actions. The team would need to train a Persistent SAE on the agent model's activations and run new tests of effects on agent behaviour.", "rubric": ["States that the paper's SAEs and causal results do not transfer directly", "Explains that the SAEs are tied to Gemma-2-2B (or Pythia) activations and the intervention effects concern the replay monitor, not the agent", "Says a new SAE trained on the agent's activations and a new behavioural test would be needed"]},
{"id": "q107", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c4"], "pair": null, "question": "Applying the paper's preprocessing for temporal statistics to a 2,000-token Pile document, how many token positions are used?", "answer": "The document is capped at 768 tokens and the first 16 positions are dropped. {"id": "q108", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c6"], "pair": null, "question": "With the paper's five MMLU subjects, what do the first five features of the supervised ranking's global ordering consist of?", "answer": "Because the subject-specific rankings are interleaved round-robin, the first five features are the top-scoring Eq. 8 feature for each of the five subjects, one per subject.", "rubric": ["States that there is one feature per subject, namely each subject's top-ranked feature", "Attributes this to the round-robin interleaving of the per-subject rankings"]},
{"id": "q109", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Under the paper's six token categories for the relative update frequency, which category do the tokens 'she', 'of' and 'but' each fall into?", "answer": "'she' is a pronoun and 'of' is an adposition, so both are function words. 'but' falls under conjunctions, which is a separate category.", "rubric": ["Assigns 'she' and 'of' to function words", "Assigns 'but' to conjunctions, which the paper lists as a category separate from function words"]},
{"id": "q110", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c3", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "If the Persistent SAE's fraction of alive features had been far below the BatchTopK baseline under matched settings, which comparisons in the evaluation would become harder to interpret?", "answer": "Comparisons at matched feature budgets, such as subject probing and monitoring, assume a similar amount of usable capacity. Fewer alive features would mean the Persistent SAE effectively has a smaller dictionary, so differences could reflect lost capacity rather than the effect of carrying state. It would also violate the principle that an extension should not degrade the decomposition.", "rubric": ["Identifies the matched-budget comparisons (probing or monitoring against the baselines) as compromised, or names the requirement not to degrade the decomposition", "Explains that differences could then reflect reduced effective capacity rather than the persistent state"]},
{"id": "q111", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c6"], "pair": null, "question": "If each of the five MMLU subjects could be identified by a single keyword appearing in every segment, which interpretation of strong spliced-probing performance would weaken?", "answer": "The interpretation that strong performance shows a representation tracking the current subject as context. A probe could succeed from local lexical cues alone. The paper chose subjects that differ in vocabulary, register and argumentative structure precisely to avoid a single lexical cue.", "rubric": ["Names the interpretation that probing reflects tracked context or subject rather than local cues", "Explains that a single keyword would let token-local lexical cues solve the task, which the choice of subjects was meant to rule out"]},
{"id": "q112", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c4"], "pair": null, "question": "If the SAE's decoder directions had turned out to be mutually orthogonal, which caveat about projection-based persistence would no longer apply, and which caveats would remain?", "answer": "The confound that a projection rises because a correlated feature is active would largely disappear. Positional drift and short-range persistence from local continuity would remain, so the prefix drop, the document cap and the control that disrupts global continuity would still be needed.", "rubric": ["States that the non-orthogonality confound (correlated features raising the projection) would no longer apply", "States that positional drift and local continuity remain as confounds"]},
{"id": "q113", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c5", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "If the shortest-timescale quintile of Persistent SAE features had scored much lower on autointerp than BatchTopK features, which claim would that undermine?", "answer": "It would undermine the claim that short-timescale features stay locally interpretable and are directly comparable to standard SAE features, since for them a ≈ h. A low score could not then be blamed on missing context outside the window, so it would suggest the persistent formulation degrades token-wise features.", "rubric": ["Identifies the claim that short-timescale features are locally interpretable or comparable to standard SAEs", "Explains that for these features a ≈ h, so the out-of-window excuse does not apply and the result points to degraded token-wise features"]},
{"id": "q114", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c6"], "pair": null, "question": "If even the supervised ranking had reached AUC no higher than random rankings at the smallest feature fractions, what would that imply for the paper's goal for persistent features?", "answer": "It would imply that subject information is not concentrated in any small set of state coordinates, even when labels choose them. That would undercut the aim of using persistent features as a small, inspectable summary of context, and would leave no headroom for a timescale ranking to show compactness.", "rubric": ["States that subject information would not be compactly concentrated in a few features", "Links this to undermining the goal of a small inspectable context summary, or to removing headroom for the timescale-versus-random comparison"]},
{"id": "q115", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c7", "c3", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "If training had collapsed the Gemma-2-2B Persistent SAE's timescales to memoryless while the Pythia one learned long timescales, which part of the evaluation would lose its basis for testing persistence?", "answer": "The prompt-injection case study, because its replay monitor uses Gemma-2-2B layer 12. With memoryless timescales, h equals a and that SAE reduces to a standard SAE. Its state could then not be tested for carrying the injection signal forward, nor could fast and slow subsets be compared.", "rubric": ["Identifies the prompt-injection monitoring and steering case study", "Explains that it relies on the Gemma layer-12 SAE, which would reduce to a standard SAE with h = a"]},
{"id": "q116", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c2", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "If the state L0 in Figure 4 had stayed at about k=20 throughout training, what would that suggest about the learned timescales?", "answer": "That features were behaving almost memorylessly. State coordinates would be non-zero only around the tokens where a feature fires, instead of persisting and accumulating beyond the token-wise budget. The persistent state would add little beyond a standard SAE.", "rubric": ["States that timescales would be effectively short or memoryless", "Explains that persistent states with longer memory would leave more non-zero coordinates than the roughly 20 active per token"]},
{"id": "q117", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper establish that long-timescale Persistent SAE features receive their new evidence mainly at punctuation and function words? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. The paper motivates the possibility from work on contextual information in punctuation and structural markers, but says the direction and strength of any relationship are an empirical matter. It defines U_{q,c} for testing this without reporting such a conclusion.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled", "Explains that the paper treats the direction of the relationship as empirical and only sets up the U_{q,c} analysis"]},
{"id": "q118", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c3", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper report that the Persistent SAE reconstructs hidden states better than BatchTopK in FVE? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. The paper states that an extension should not degrade reconstruction and lists FVE and cosine similarity as metrics. Its text reports no comparative FVE values; Figure 4 shows only Persistent SAE training loss and state L0.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled", "Explains that FVE is set as a requirement or protocol metric but no comparison showing superiority is reported"]},
{"id": "q119", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c6"], "pair": null, "question": "Because the subject probing includes a supervised ranking, was the Persistent SAE exposed to MMLU subject labels in training? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Contradicted. The SAEs are trained only on Pile activations, and MMLU is never used for training. Labels enter only in the Eq. 8 score used to order features for the probe, computed after training as a reference point.", "rubric": ["Answers contradicted", "Explains that labels are used only post hoc for the supervised ordering or probe, while SAE training uses Pile data without labels"]},
{"id": "q120", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c7"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the AUC of 0.51 from the monitor's yes-minus-no logit show that Gemma-2-2B's layer-12 hidden states carry no information about the injection? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not supported. The 0.51 measures only the model's prompted answer. Whether the hidden states contain injection information is tested separately by the internal linear probes, which is exactly why the paper trains them rather than relying on prompting.", "rubric": ["Answers that the claim is not supported (not settled or contradicted is acceptable, but not supported)", "Explains that 0.51 concerns the prompted output, whereas internal information is assessed by separate probes on the hidden states"]},
{"id": "q121", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c1", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Can a Persistent SAE feature's state take negative values to encode evidence against the feature? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Contradicted. Both a(t) and h(t) are defined in the non-negative orthant. The state integrates non-negative sparse updates and is kept on the scale of those activations, so it cannot go negative.", "rubric": ["Answers contradicted", "Explains that a(t) and h(t) are non-negative by definition, since the state integrates non-negative activations"]},
{"id": "q122", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c3"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the matched setup ensure that the Temporal SAE reads exactly 2,048 hidden-state activations per step, like BatchTopK? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled, and likely not. The paper matches the number of reconstructed token positions per step, but the Temporal SAE's buffer returns previous–next pairs. It therefore also reads previous-token activations, and the paper says matching holds only up to the pairing its objective requires.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled or not guaranteed", "Explains that only reconstructed positions are matched, while pairs bring in extra previous-token activations"]},
{"id": "q123", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c6"], "pair": null, "question": "Is the supervised ranking guaranteed to be the best possible feature ordering for the linear probe at each budget? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not supported. It scores each feature independently by its mean-state difference for one subject, then interleaves the subjects round-robin. This ignores scale, variance and redundancy among features. The paper calls it a label-informed reference, not an optimal selection.", "rubric": ["Answers that this is not supported or not guaranteed", "Explains that the ranking uses per-feature mean differences (Eq. 8) with round-robin interleaving, which ignores variance and redundancy, so it is a reference rather than an optimum"]}
]}
